newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Market drop brings out put buyers.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Market drop brings out put buyers.

text.p: Early S&P 100 index OEX call buying gave way to put buying as the underlying market succumbed to profit taking, options traders said Wednesday.
"We had a lot of call buyers earlier, but it's slowly slipped away," said Jack Callahan, an independent market maker in OEX options.
As the market continued to decline, put buyers emerged.
"Today that run for 8,000 (on the Dow industrial average DJI was a little too obvious and we ran into a little bit of traffic this morning," Callahan said.
By about 1330 CDT/1830 GMT, the Dow was down 75 points at roughly 7,888.
The blue chip barometer closed at a record 7,962.31 on Tuesday and rallied to 7,991 early Wednesday before backing off.
The OEX, which closed Tuesday at 897.24, fell 6.84 to 890.40 and the S&P 500 index .SPX was down 5.37 at 913.38. September S&P 500 futures lost 7.40 to 920.40.
"With the futures dropping, the stock market sold off and puts are finding new interest here," Callahan said.
The renewed put interest helped pump volatilities back up.
The volatility index VIX, which is calculated off certain OEX contracts, was up 1.61, or 7.6 percent, at 22.75. It reached 23.01 intraday.
One trader noted that although investors were buying index puts, pushing up premiums and volatility, there was no sense of panic or sentiment that the market had seen its top.
Jerry Hegarty, an options analyst at Thomson Financial Services, said in an intraday report that index put volume was solidly outpacing index call volume, a bullish sign.
"This should eventually lead to a solid rally which takes prices to new highs within the next three days," he said.
Hegarty added, however, that a late session recovery would be important for the market's ability to bounce higher.
Such a recovery was looking less likely as trading wore one, with stock prices extending losses with less than an hour of trading to go.
September S&P 500 futures fell their initial 15-point daily limit and the New York Stock Exchange set "sidecar" trading curbs as the Dow fell more than 100.
